draft.title: Tangents and normals
card: The gradient of the tangent at x = a is f'(a). Find f(a) for the point, then use y − y₁ = m(x − x₁) with m = f'(a).
The normal is the line through the same point, perpendicular to the tangent. Its gradient is the negative reciprocal: −1/f'(a), when f'(a) is not 0.
Example: f(x) = x², at x = 3. The point is (3, 9) and f'(x) = 2x, so the tangent gradient is 6. Tangent: y − 9 = 6(x − 3), so y = 6x − 9.
The normal gradient is −1/6, so the normal is y − 9 = −1/6(x − 3).
draft.remember: Use f'(a) for the tangent gradient, then flip it and change the sign for the normal.

a.q: The tangent to a curve at a point has gradient 4. What is the gradient of the normal at that point?
a.why: The normal is perpendicular to the tangent, so its gradient is the negative reciprocal of 4, which is −1/4. The option 1/4 flips the gradient but keeps the sign, so the product is 1/4, not −1.
a.clue: Flip the number, then change the sign.

b.q: What is the equation of the tangent to f(x) = x² + 2x at x = 1?
b.why: f(1) = 3, so the point is (1, 3). f'(x) = 2x + 2, so the gradient is 4. Then y − 3 = 4(x − 1), giving y = 4x − 1. The option y = 4x + 3 uses the right gradient but wrongly takes the y-value as the intercept.
b.clue: Find the point and f'(1) first, then use y − y₁ = m(x − x₁).

problems.detail: Why (a) says the product of 4 and 1/4 is 1/4. It is actually 1, not 1/4, and this is the reason it is not −1.
The normal equation is written 'y − 9 = −1/6(x − 3)'. In inline slash notation this can be read as −1/(6(x − 3)). Writing −(1/6)(x − 3) would be clearer.

check.summary: Both questions have a single correct answer, and the card's maths is right. Why (a) wrongly says 4 × 1/4 is 1/4 (it is 1), and the card's normal equation would be clearer with brackets around −1/6.
